newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: WEEK AHEAD - Judgment day nears for Australian rates.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD - Judgment day nears for Australian rates.

text.p: The latest waiting game for interest rates could be over this week, with markets gearing up for a possible monetary policy easing as early as Friday.
The key releases of the week are June quarter inflation on Wednesday and May quarter wages data on Thursday, both of which are expected to clear the way for a fifth cut.

"We expect both releases to meet, if not exceed, present bullish expectations," Commonwealth Bank economist Tim Moloney said. The official cash rate is 5.50 percent, having been reduced on four occasions over the past year from 7.50 percent.
The June quarter consumer price index is forecast to fall 0.1 percent in the quarter, and rise 0.5 percent over the year.
If the CPI is negative, it will be the first quarter of deflation since June 1992, and the lowest annual inflation rate since the year to December quarter 1992.

The underlying rate of inflation is expected to fall to its lowest annual level since the series' inception in the early 1970s. If the quarterly result comes in as forecast, it will mean that in five out of the last six quarters, underlying inflation has been 0.5 percent or less.
The Reserve Bank targets the underlying rate, aiming to keep it to between two and three percent over a run of years, so the forecast is seen as very bullish.
Average weekly ordinary time earnings (AWOTE) data are expected to show the lowest quarterly rise in over one year.
That will see the annual rate moderate from the February quarter's 4.3 percent, and further away from the level seen as the RBA's speed limit on wages, 4.5 percent.

Apart from inflation, the RBA also has an employment objective and analysts said a low inflation and moderate wages result would give the RBA room to ease rates as a means of stimulating employment growth.

"With labour market conditions remaining very weak in mid 1997, inflation expectations at record lows, and the government under intense pressure to do something to get the economy moving, the RBA will be under some pressure to cut rates," Westpac senior economist John Peters said.
AUSTRALIAN DOLLAR (Fri: US$0.7390/95, NY $0.7400/10)

The dollar has been under pressure from the prospect of another rate cut, having fallen to an 18-month low last week, and unable to sustain a sizeable rally while the speculation about a cut remains. While a late Friday surge above US$0.7380 was a positive, the dollar needs to break above US$0.7430 to reverse some of the current negative sentiment, and keep it clear of the US$0.7310 low of last week.

"Ordinarily you would suggest that low inflation should be warmly welcomed by currency markets," the Commonwealth's Moloney said. "However, it is unlikely that currency markets will take the time to reward the Australian dollar for its low inflation status until it can clearly see Australia's easing cycle in the rear view mirror," he said.
That may be closer than previously thought, with analysts talking of an expected lift in activity in the latter stages of 1997 and traders said a fifth cut was well factored in.
"I think we're getting to the point of factoring in only one cut, but it is well factored in," said Steve North, head of foreign exchange at Chase Manhattan.
If there is no rate cut, the risks for the Australian dollar are to the topside, analysts said.
"If it is not delivered, a rebound to US$0.75 is expected," said Craig James, senior economist at Colonial State Bank.
AUSTRALIAN BONDS (Fri: 10-year yield 6.61 pct, 3 year 5.70)
The bond market could see its strong rally from April continue this week if the second quarter inflation and wages data proves as modest as expected and spark a further spread contraction to the U.S.

"With inflation likely to remain low over the next year, combined with the continued disappointing performance of the real economy, the RBA is likely to reduce official interest rates by a further 50 basis points," said Peter Munckton, senior economist at Bankers Trust.
Munckton said the most likely timing of a rate cut in current official 5.5 percent interest rates would be after the August RBA board meeting.

Although a Reuters poll of economists taken on Friday found expectations for the Australian/U.S. 10-year bond yield spread at year-end centring on a median 50 basis points compared to the current level of 40 bp, some see a test of parity before then.
This would be largely as a result of Australia's much superior inflation performance over the U.S.

At one stage last week the September 10-year bond futures contract struck a fresh 3-1/2 year high of 93.510, taking the cash yield down to around 6.50 percent and keeping the market on track for a test of the all time high 93.630 sent in early 1994.
The contract was first listed on the Sydney Futures Exchange in December 1984.

However, the Reuters poll also found median expectations for the 10-year bond yield at year-end backing up to 7.05 percent, with some economists expecting the easing cycle to be finished by then and the market beginning to worry about tighter policy and inflation during 1998.

The market will start the week with a softer bias after U.S. Treasuries ended weaker on Friday as positions were lightened ahead of Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan's semi-annual Humphrey-Hawkins testimony next week.
The U.S. 30-year bond closed at 101-10/32, down 14/32 from Thursday. Its yield rose to 6.52 percent from 6.49 percent.
AUSTRALIAN STOCKS (Fri: All Ords 2,684.2, up 14.5)
Australian stocks are likely to start the week with a weak tone following the 130 point fall on Wall Street as the U.S. market retreated from its dizzying heights.

Local issues are dominated by the second quarter inflation data, due Wednesday, which may satisfy the market's craving for another interest rate cut. The general tone looks reasonably firm, but no-one is likely to be brave ahead of the data.
"It looks okay but really I can't see much happening until we get the inflation figures," said a dealer at a Sydney-based investment bank, a sentiment echoed by others.

"That will be the issue. The market was reasonably directionless last week as far as economic news goes, and this week figures come out that we will be focussing closely on," said Daiwa Securities dealer Michael Sichlau.

In corporate news, the market will be watching pay TV operator Australis Media for details of its long mooted merger with rival Foxtel, jointly owned by News Corp and government-owned telcommunications carrier, Telstra Corp.
Macquarie Bank holds its annual meeting on Wednesday while Fosters Brewing holds its meeting on Thursday to approve the recent BHP/Asahi selloff deal.
National Australia Bank is due to report its third quarter results on Thursday.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
